result.summary: Jupiter calls a council where Venus and Juno quarrel and he declares himself neutral. Æneas sails back with the Etruscan fleet, is met by the ship-nymphs, and lands to relieve the camp. Pallas dies at Turnus's hand, Juno spirits Turnus away with a phantom, and Æneas kills Lausus and then Mezentius.

scenes.title: Council of the gods
scenes.summary: Jupiter rebukes the gods; Venus and Juno plead for their sides. Jupiter declares neutrality and lets destiny decide.
scenes.stakes: Venus fears for the Trojans and Ascanius; Juno defends Turnus and the Rutulians.

scenes.title: Camp besieged; Æneas sails
scenes.summary: The Trojan camp is hard pressed with Ascanius among the defenders, while Æneas, having gained Tarchon's alliance, sails by night.
scenes.stakes: The besieged Trojans may be overrun and destroyed.

scenes.title: Catalogue of Etruscan allies
scenes.summary: The poet lists the Etruscan and other leaders and their ships following Æneas.

scenes.title: The ship-nymphs warn Æneas
scenes.summary: Cymodoce and the transformed ships warn Æneas and urge him to arm. His shield blazes as he nears the shore.
scenes.stakes: Ascanius and the camp are in danger.

scenes.title: Landing and battle on the shore
scenes.summary: Turnus tries to stop the landing; Tarchon's ship is wrecked while Æneas kills many Latins.
scenes.stakes: Both sides risk defeat in the landing fight.

scenes.title: Death of Pallas
scenes.summary: Pallas rallies the Arcadians and fights Turnus after praying to Hercules. Turnus kills him and takes his belt.
scenes.stakes: Pallas risks his life; his death will bring Evander grief and Turnus doom.

scenes.title: Æneas's rampage
scenes.summary: Æneas, vowing vengeance, spares none and kills Magus, Lucagus and Liger, then frees the camp.
scenes.stakes: Æneas's enemies face death; he seeks Turnus.

scenes.title: Juno's phantom saves Turnus
scenes.summary: Juno gets Jupiter's partial consent and lures Turnus onto a ship with a phantom Æneas. He is carried to Ardea in shame.

scenes.title: Mezentius and Lausus
scenes.summary: Mezentius fights fiercely until wounded by Æneas. Lausus dies saving him, and Mezentius then rides out, is felled, and welcomes death.
scenes.stakes: Mezentius risks death and the loss of his son.

alias_notes.explanation: Alternate form of the same god's name.

notable_quotes.reason: Jupiter declares his impartiality: 'Jove, as king, is alike to all.'
Narrator's comment on human blindness to fate after Turnus takes Pallas's belt.

analysis.text: Fate, divine neutrality and human responsibility meet: Jupiter lets destiny work while mortals suffer.
Pietas appears in Lausus and Mezentius, and Æneas's pity for Lausus contrasts with his vengeful rage after Pallas.

legacy.text: Æneas's killing of Turnus, prepared by Pallas's death and the belt, shaped later debate about mercy and vengeance in epic.

fun_facts.text: The catalogue of Etruscan allies, including Mantua's founding by Ocnus, honours Virgil's own birthplace region near Mantua.

language_notes.text: Dardans are the Trojans, named after their ancestor Dardanus; Latium is the region of Italy where Rome would rise.
Refers to Hannibal's invasion of Italy through the Alps in the Punic Wars, centuries later.
Tydeus' son is Diomedes, a Greek hero who fought at Troy and settled at Arpi in Italy; he wounded Venus in the Iliad.
Bitterly ironic: Venus recalls that Diomedes once wounded her, saying her wounds are 'yet in the future'.
Recalls earlier troubles of the Trojans: the burned fleet in Sicily, and Juno's storm sent through Aeolus, king of the winds.
Amathus, Paphos, Cythera and Idalia were Cyprian and nearby sites sacred to Venus.
Cassandra was the Trojan prophetess doomed never to be believed; Juno sneers that Aeneas follows her 'mad' prophecies.
Pilumnus and Venilia were Italian divinities, so Turnus is of divine descent on his native soil.
Leman means lover; the Dardan leman is Paris, who took Helen to Troy and caused the Trojan War.
Jupiter swears by the river Styx, the most binding oath for gods. His brother is Pluto, lord of the underworld.
"Belt the ramparts with flame" means to encircle the walls with fire.
"Unavailing wretchedness": their misery achieves nothing. Line numbers from the source edition are scattered through the text and can be ignored.
"Orician terebinth": wood of the terebinth tree, from Oricum, prized for inlay work. Dardany means Troy's land; the boy is Ascanius.
Pactolus was a Lydian river famed for gold-bearing sands; Ismarus is Lydian, so the river marks his homeland.
Mnestheus' "yesterday's triumph" refers to his earlier repulse of Turnus from the rampart, when Turnus broke into the camp.
"Freed from the spell of destiny": an oracle had forbidden the Etruscans to follow a native leader, so they await a foreign one.
Ida is the Trojan mountain; Cybele, whose lions draw her chariot, was its goddess, so the ship's emblems honor her.
Helicon is the Muses' mountain in Boeotia; the poet asks the Muses to open it like a spring of inspiration. The goddesses are the Muses.
"Brass-sheathed Tiger" refers to the ship's name and figurehead; ships in the catalogue are named for their emblems. "Sheaf" means a bundle of arrows.
The Chalybes were a people famed for working iron; here their name stands for iron mines, as Ilva (Elba) was known for iron.
Asilas is a seer using the Etruscan arts: reading entrails of sacrificed victims, stars, bird-calls and lightning to learn the gods' will.
Pisa was said to be founded by settlers from Pisa in Elis, near the river Alpheus in Greece; hence "sprung from Alpheus."
"Cognizance" means a heraldic badge or emblem; here the swan plumage on the helmet recalls their father's transformation.
Cycnus mourned Phaethon, who died driving the Sun's chariot; Phaethon's sisters became poplars, and Cycnus was turned into a swan. "Eld" means age, here the swan's down.
Mezentius, the cruel Etruscan king, had been expelled by his own people, who therefore send swords against him; the Mincius is a river personified.
Dian is Diana, the moon goddess; her "night-flying steeds" draw her chariot, the moon, across the sky. "Cope" means vault or canopy.
"Bevy" means a group; "erst" means formerly, and "brazen" means bronze-covered.
The ships were built from pines of Mount Ida, sacred to Cybele. Æneas's fleet was turned into sea-nymphs in an earlier episode, when Turnus tried to burn it.
"The false Rutulian" is Turnus, who attacked the ships with fire. The nymphs "burst your bonds" by breaking their moorings.
The Arcadian horse are Evander's men, allied with the Etruscans under Tarchon. Turnus plans to intercept them before they reach the Trojan camp.
The Fire-god is Vulcan, who forged Æneas's divine armour at Venus's request. "Marge" means border.
Æneas invokes Cybele, "mother of the gods," with her cult places Ida and Dindymus. Her chariot was drawn by lions, and the ships had been her gift.
"Sequacious" means following one after another, describing the cranes' clamour. Strymon is a Thracian river where cranes were said to winter.
The Sirian blaze is Sirius, the Dog Star, whose rising in late summer was thought to bring drought and sickness.
The War-god is Mars; the saying means a brave man's hand is where Mars chooses to dwell, so courage brings divine favour.
"Carry them home" means drive the ships firmly onto the shore; "this land that hates you" means hostile Latium.
"Scatheless" means unharmed.
"Presage" means an omen or foretelling; Æneas's first charge signals how the fight will go.
Lycus was delivered by caesarean section after his mother died, and so was dedicated to Apollo, the god of healing and birth.
Alicides is Hercules, grandson of Alceus. Melampus had followed him through his labours, and his sons Cisseus and Gyas carry Herculean clubs.
"Dardan" means Trojan, from Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojans.
Boreas is the north wind, thought to dwell in Thrace; the three Thracians claim descent from him.
Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy.
Latium is the region of Italy around Rome, here standing for the Latin and Rutulian forces opposing the Arcadians.
"Conjure" means solemnly entreat or appeal to by something sacred, here the name of Evander and past victories.
"Shall the sea or Troy be our goal?" means: will we reach the sea (and drown) or the Trojan camp, which is the only way to safety.
"Stepdame's couch": Anchemolus had committed incest with his stepmother, so the poet marks him as guilty.
"Fire-god" is Vulcan, used by metonymy for fire itself.
Father Tiber is the river god of the Tiber. Pallas promises to hang Halesus' arms on an oak sacred to him.
Alcides is Hercules, grandson of Alceus. He had once been a guest of Evander, which is why Pallas appeals to him.
The Almighty Father is Jove (the Greek Zeus), father of Hercules, who comforts his son about Pallas's doomed fate.
The belt shows the Danaids, who killed their husbands on their wedding night. Its crime foreshadows Turnus's own guilt.
Teucrians: the Trojans, named after their ancestor Teucer; here the besieged Trojan camp is meant.
Victims for the dead: Æneas takes captives to sacrifice at Pallas's funeral pyre, a human sacrifice in the manner of Homer's Patroclus.
"Trading usages of war" means the custom of sparing captives for ransom; Turnus ended it by killing Pallas without mercy.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, god of war, to whom the spoils are dedicated as a trophy.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose."
Ægæon (Briareus) was a hundred-handed giant who, in legend, fought against Jove (Jupiter) and his thunderbolts.
Liger boasts that Æneas faces no Greek foes such as Diomede or Achilles, whose horses and chariot Æneas had known at Troy.
"Laid bare the seat of breath" means he pierced the chest and exposed the lungs.
"Sister mine and sweetest wife in one": Jupiter and Juno are both siblings and spouses in myth; the line is affectionate but edged with teasing.
Teucrian means Trojan, from Teucer, an early king of Troy; Juno uses it for Æneas's followers.
"Doomed youth" and "destiny that presses on his heels": Jupiter allows only a delay of Turnus's fated death, not an escape from it.
Dardan means Trojan, from Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojan royal line.
"Promised bridal" refers to Æneas's betrothal to Lavinia, which Turnus himself had hoped to win.
Osinius was a king of Clusium, an Etruscan city, allied with Æneas. His ship is taken by Turnus's pursuit.
"Saturn's daughter" is Juno, daughter of Saturn.
Hecuba (daughter of Cisseus), pregnant with Paris, dreamed she bore a firebrand that would burn Troy. Paris was born the same night as Mimas.
"Wight" is an archaic word for a person; "Grecian wight" means a Greek man.
"Pæan" is a song of triumph or thanksgiving, originally addressed to Apollo.
Mezentius scorns the gods; he means Jove will have to settle his fate himself, as he fears no one else.
Tisiphone is one of the Furies, avenging spirits of the underworld, here shown spreading frenzy among the dead and dying.
"The god of my worship" shows Mezentius's contempt for the gods; he worships only his own strength and weapon.
The "fatal sisters" are the Fates, who spin and cut the thread of each person's life.
Æneas speaks to the dead Lausus: he returns his armour and his body to his ancestors' shades, 'if that be aught to you now' meaning if the dead can care.
'Stanching' means stopping the flow of blood from wounds; Mezentius is washing his wound in the Tiber.
Mezentius was a tyrant driven from his Etruscan throne by his subjects; his exile made Lausus share his guilt and enemies.
'I ween' is archaic for 'I think' or 'I believe'; 'Teucrian' means Trojan.
'Charged his two hands' means he armed both hands, filling them with javelins.
Mezentius says he will neither fear death nor show reverence to any god, in keeping with his contempt for the gods.
'Springs from his covert' means Æneas darts out from behind the cover of his shield.
'The Tuscan' is Mezentius, an Etruscan king; Tuscany is the Roman name for Etruria.

context_notes.text: Venus is Aeneas' mother and champions the Trojans; Juno, Jupiter's wife, opposes them throughout the poem.
Xanthus and Simois are rivers near Troy; Ilium is another name for Troy.
Juno refers to Venus rescuing Aeneas from Greeks in Troy's fall, and to his ships turned into sea nymphs, which happened earlier in this book's tale.
This is a catalogue of Trojan defenders, many with Asian origins like Lycia, reflecting Troy's allies.
Venus is Æneas' mother and thus Ascanius' grandmother, which explains her special care for the boy.
Pallas is the young son of Evander, sent with Æneas as ally and learner of war.
Epic poets traditionally invoke the Muses before a catalogue of warriors; this list of Etruscan allies follows that convention.
Gravisca's "tainted air" refers to the unhealthy, malarial coastal marshes of Etruria.
Mantua, Virgil's home region, is described as founded by Ocnus, son of the prophetess Manto; it has three races and Etruscan ruling strength.
Cymodoce is a sea-nymph, one of the Nereids in Roman tradition. Here she is the transformed ships' spokeswoman.
Anchises was Æneas's father. Calling him Anchises' line gives his lineage; "Trojan" and "Teucrians" and "Dardans" all name the Trojans.
Tarchon is the Etruscan leader allied with Æneas against the Latins.
Teucrians is another name for the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer.
Venus is Æneas's mother, so she protects him and his men by turning aside some of the darts.
Achates is Æneas's loyal companion. The Rutulians are Turnus's people.
Pallas is the young son of Evander, king of the Arcadian settlers, and fights as an ally of Æneas. His men are normally cavalry.
Turnus's sister is the nymph Juturna, who helps her brother in the war.
Sarpedon, a son of Jove and a Trojan ally, was killed by Patroclus at Troy, although Jove had wished to save him.
Pallas was Evander's son and Æneas's young ally, killed by Turnus earlier in this book; Evander had hosted Æneas at his table.
Phœbus is Apollo and Trivia is Diana (Hecate), so Hæmonides serves both deities as priest.
Faunus was an Italian woodland god; Tarquitus's descent from a nymph and a god adds to his pride.
Daunus is Turnus's father; Juno wants to send his son back to him alive.
Ardea was the chief town of Turnus's people, the Rutulians, and the seat of Daunus.
Mezentius is the exiled Etruscan (Tyrrhene) tyrant, hated for cruelty, who fights for Turnus against Æneas and the Trojans (Teucrians).
Orion was a giant hunter of Greek myth; Nereus is a sea-god, here standing for the sea.
Antores had followed Hercules from Argos and then joined Evander, the Arcadian king allied with Æneas.
Lausus is Mezentius's young son, noted for his devotion to his father despite the father's cruelty.
Mezentius, the exiled Etruscan king, has been wounded by Æneas and withdrawn from the fighting to the river's bank.
Rhæbus is Mezentius' horse, his loyal companion in war, to whom he speaks as to a comrade.
Apollo was the god of prophecy, archery and healing, and is invoked here as a patron of Troy.
Proper burial was essential in the ancient world, since the unburied dead could not find rest.

literary_notes.text: Venus addresses Jupiter directly with exalted titles, flattering him while preparing her complaint.
Venus bitterly asks that Troy's suffering be repeated, showing how pointless the Trojans' long toil seems to her.
Juno turns Venus's own acts of divine rescue into a charge of hypocrisy against her.
The gods' murmuring is likened to rising winds in a forest, which warn the sailor of a coming storm.
Heaven, earth, the winds and Ocean seem to hush and tremble in reverence, showing Jupiter's overwhelming authority.
Destiny is given a will and a way of her own, ending Jupiter's speech with a stern, neutral line.
Ascanius' shining head is compared to a jewel in gold and to ivory inlaid in wood, stressing his beauty and preciousness.
The narrator turns to address Ismarus directly, giving the catalogue of warriors immediacy and honoring him.
The shift from siege to Æneas at sea marks a cut between simultaneous scenes, joining the two storylines.
Æneas brooding while Pallas asks eager questions shows the leader's burden against the youth's curiosity.
The poet turns directly to the Muses, addressing them as present to ask for the power to narrate.
Virgil addresses the warriors directly, giving the catalogue a personal, tender touch.
The ship's Centaur figurehead seems alive, standing threatening over the water and hurling a rock.
The Triton figurehead is drawn vividly, half man and half sea beast, with the roaring wave beneath its body.
Dian "trampling" the sky with steeds, and care that "refuses slumber," turn night and worry into acting beings.
The ship's speed is compared to darts and arrows, stressing the nymph's divine power.
The Trojans' shout is likened to cranes crying as they flee the south wind, suggesting a noisy, flying host.
Æneas's blazing helmet and shield are compared to ominous comets and the Dog Star, making him seem both awe-inspiring and a portent of death.
The hand is imagined as the god's chosen seat, as though Mars dwells in the brave man's arm.
The narrator turns to address Tarchon directly, which lends pathos to his ship's wreck.
The sword "devours" the side, making the weapon a hungry creature and emphasizing the violence.
The narrator speaks to Cydon, which gives sympathy to his doomed pursuit of Clytius.
The battle is compared to winds and storm-clouds in equal contest, conveying how evenly the two armies are matched.
The spreading fire driven by wind and watched by a proud shepherd compares the Arcadians' growing ardor around Pallas to a conquering blaze.
Turnus is compared to a lion eyeing a bull, which presents him as a predator and Pallas as its prey.
The narrator breaks in with a general reflection on human blindness to fate, judging Turnus's pride before the reader sees its result.
The poet predicts that Turnus will regret taking the belt, anticipating his death at the hands of Æneas.
The narrator addresses the dead Pallas directly, deepening the pathos of the youth's single day of battle.
The narrator suddenly addresses Turnus directly, heightening the sense that Æneas's rage is aimed at him.
Æneas's cold, swift killing of a suppliant shows how grief and vengeance have overwhelmed his usual piety and mercy.
Comparing Æneas to the hundred-armed giant Ægæon conveys his superhuman, overwhelming fury on the battlefield.
Æneas mocks Lucagus by turning Liger's boast about the horses into a taunt that Lucagus himself abandoned them.
Likening Æneas to a torrent or dark storm presents his slaughter as an unstoppable natural force.
The phantom is compared to ghosts and dreams, stressing that it is insubstantial and deceptive.
Turnus believes he is pursuing victory, but the winds are carrying his triumph away; he is the one deceived.
Turnus addresses Jupiter and the winds, who cannot answer, showing his despair and shame.
Turnus's honour-bound impulse toward suicide or swimming back shows his pride, while Juno's restraint shows her protectiveness.
Mezentius is likened to a rock braving wind and sea, stressing his unshaken, stubborn endurance against the massed attackers.
Mezentius becomes a boar at bay, hunted from afar; the image shows his savage courage and the cowardice of attackers.
The narrator turns to address the dead Lausus directly, promising to preserve his memory and honoring his sacrifice.
Æneas enduring the javelins is compared to farmers sheltering from a hailstorm, turning battle into weather and patient waiting.
The mother's golden embroidery on the pierced tunic makes the youth's death more tender and tragic.
Mezentius' self-reproach in a string of questions shows his grief and guilt, and a rare tenderness in a man known as cruel.
Despite his wound, Mezentius rises to ride out unflinching, showing the defiant courage that defines him.
The javelins stuck in Æneas' shield are imagined as a vast grove growing from the bronze, making the shield a forest.
The vivid picture of his blood streaming over his armour ends his death with stark, defiant finality.
